title: What is RAG
content: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that enhances large language models by retrieving relevant documents from an external knowledge base before generating a response. Instead of relying solely on parametric knowledge baked into model weights during training, RAG allows models to access up-to-date, domain-specific information at inference time. The retrieval step typically uses vector similarity search, where both the query and documents are embedded into a high-dimensional space and matched by cosine similarity. This approach significantly reduces hallucinations because the model is grounded in real retrieved facts.

title: Vector Search Basics
content: Vector search (also called semantic search or approximate nearest neighbor search) enables finding documents that are semantically similar to a query, even when they don't share exact keywords. Each document is encoded into a dense vector using an embedding model such as BERT, Sentence-BERT, or OpenAI text-embedding. At query time, the query is embedded with the same model and the database returns the top-k vectors closest by cosine distance or dot product. Popular vector databases include Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, and pgvector (a PostgreSQL extension). The main limitation of pure vector search is that it can miss exact keyword matches that BM25 would catch.

title: BM25 and Sparse Retrieval
content: BM25 (Best Match 25) is a classical ranking function used in information retrieval systems like Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. It is based on TF-IDF (term frequency-inverse document frequency) with additional normalization for document length. BM25 excels at exact keyword matching and is highly efficient. It does not require GPU or embedding models. The main weakness of BM25 is that it cannot handle synonyms or paraphrases — it only matches on exact token overlap. Hybrid retrieval combines BM25 (sparse) and vector (dense) search to get the best of both worlds: semantic understanding plus exact keyword precision.

title: Hybrid Search and Reciprocal Rank Fusion
content: Hybrid search combines sparse retrieval (BM25) and dense retrieval (vector search) to improve recall and precision. The most popular merging strategy is Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which assigns each document a score of 1/(k + rank) where k is a constant (usually 60) and rank is the document's position in each ranked list. Documents appearing in both lists get higher combined scores. RRF is robust because it does not require calibrating the scale of scores from different systems. Studies show hybrid search with RRF consistently outperforms either method alone, especially on out-of-domain queries.

title: Cross-Encoder Reranking
content: Reranking is a second-stage retrieval step that re-scores retrieved candidates using a more powerful but slower model. A cross-encoder takes the (query, document) pair as a single input and outputs a relevance score, unlike bi-encoders which embed query and document independently. Cross-encoders are much more accurate because they can model query-document interaction directly, but they are too slow to compare against all documents in a large corpus. The typical pipeline is: retrieve top-50 candidates with fast bi-encoder + BM25, then rerank with cross-encoder to get the final top-5. Popular reranking models include ms-marco-MiniLM and Cohere Rerank.

title: Chunking Strategies
content: Chunking is the process of splitting documents into smaller pieces before embedding and indexing. The choice of chunk size significantly affects RAG quality. Small chunks (128-256 tokens) improve precision — retrieved text is focused on a single concept. Large chunks (512-1024 tokens) provide more context but may include irrelevant information. Overlapping chunks (adding 10-20% overlap between adjacent chunks) reduces the risk of cutting important sentences at boundaries. Advanced chunking strategies include recursive character splitting, semantic chunking (split at sentence boundaries based on embedding similarity drop), and hierarchical indexing (summary + detail levels).

title: Embedding Models Comparison
content: Embedding models transform text into dense vectors. Key metrics are: vector dimension (higher = more expressive but slower), max token length (longer documents need models with larger context), and benchmark scores on MTEB. Popular free models: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384 dims, fast, good for short texts), all-mpnet-base-v2 (768 dims, higher quality), BGE-M3 (supports 100+ languages). Commercial options: OpenAI text-embedding-3-small (1536 dims), Cohere embed-v3. For production RAG systems, the embedding model choice is often more impactful than the LLM choice, because retrieval quality is the bottleneck.

title: RAG Evaluation Metrics
content: Evaluating RAG systems requires measuring both retrieval quality and generation quality. Key metrics: (1) Context Recall — what fraction of relevant information was retrieved; (2) Context Precision — what fraction of retrieved chunks were relevant; (3) Faithfulness — is the generated answer grounded in the retrieved context (no hallucinations); (4) Answer Similarity — semantic similarity between generated and reference answer; (5) Answer Correctness — factual accuracy. Frameworks like RAGAS, TruLens, and DeepEval automate these evaluations. Latency and cost per query are additional operational metrics. A common failure mode is high answer similarity but low faithfulness — the model answers from parametric memory instead of the context.
